THOUGHT: The patient is a 57-year-old male with a 6-month-old non-healing ulcer on the right lower leg, chronic bilateral leg edema (worse on the right) for over a decade, a prior DVT in the same leg 5 years ago, and a strong family history of similar leg problems—suggesting a hereditary or chronic venous disorder. Physical exam reveals varicose veins, skin discoloration (hyperpigmentation), and signs of chronic venous insufficiency (CVI), including edema and diminished but palpable distal pulses (ruling out acute arterial occlusion). Doppler ultrasound confirms venous reflux and obstruction in both superficial and deep systems—consistent with post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), a common sequela of DVT. The wound culture is negative, making active infection unlikely; normal CBC argues against systemic inflammation or hematologic malignancy. Absence of diabetes, neuropathy, or arterial insufficiency (pulses present) makes diabetic foot ulcer or critical limb ischemia less likely. The chronicity, location (gaiter area), hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis (implied by skin changes), and venous pathology all point to a venous leg ulcer—the most common type of chronic wound in adults with CVI/PTS. Family history may suggest underlying genetic thrombophilia or familial venous valve incompetence, but the dominant clinical picture is chronic venous hypertension leading to tissue breakdown.

DIAGNOSIS: Venous leg ulcer
